name: Kemant
confidence_why: Hetzron 1976 (reporting Sasse's field notes) and Appleyard 1991 (the Kemant fieldworker) both describe Kemant as having stress rather than tone and neither gives the position of the stress, while Zelealem 2000, Halévy 1873, Reinisch 1885 and Flad 1869 say nothing about it, so the record rests on two agreeing but thin statements and the placement is unreported rather than disputed.

catalog_quote: Both Bilin and Awngi are tone languages while Kemant has only stress. Inadequate work on the other Agaw tongues makes it impossible to make any statement about tone elsewhere. [...] In Kemant, all words have stress in isolation, but some may lose it in context. This may also be a trace of an older tonal system. [Hetzron 1976: 12] [...] Note that the Kemant plural suffixes are all stressed. [Hetzron 1976: 16] || only two Agaw languages (Awngi and Bilin) appear to have a tonal accent system comparable with LEC, whilst the other languages that have been studied in recent years (Kemant and Khamtanga) may have moved, or be moving towards a predictable, syllable-counting stress-based system, perhaps under the influence of Ethiopian Semitic. [Appleyard 1991: 10] || The suprasegmental features are those which operate on longer stretches of speech, such as length of consonants and vowels, stress, tone, relative timing and rhythm, intonation, pitch and voice quality [...]. Among such features, some of them will be considered in this section. 1.8.2.1 Consonant Gemination [Tsige 2009: 12] || 5.1.1.3 Suprasegmentals 5.1.1.3.1 Gemination There is consonant gemination as a phonetic feature occurring rarely. [...] As an Agew language, there is no vowel length in Kemantney. [...] 5.1.1.4 The Syllable Structure In indigenous words, two open and two closed syllable types have been identified (see also Appleyard, 1975). They are V, CV, VC and CVC. [Zelealem 2000: 161-162]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (52 pp., archive.org HetzronTheAgawLanguages1976), rendered pp. 14 and 18 to images and read them. p. 14 = issue p. 12 = 'AAL 3, 42', section 4.1.3 PROSODY: 'Both Bilin and Awngi are tone languages while Kemant has only stress. Inadequate work on the other Agaw tongues makes it impossible to make any statement about tone elsewhere.'.. 'In Kemant, all words have stress in isolation, but some may lose it in context. This may also be a trace of an older tonal system.' p. 18 = issue p. 16 = 'AAL 3, 46', in 4.2.1.1 plural formation: 'Note that the Kemant plural suffixes are all stressed.' All three sentences are on the page scan exactly as quoted; locator…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kemant is described as a stress language, not a tone language: every word carries a stress in isolation, but some words lose it in connected speech (which Hetzron reads as a possible relic of an older tonal system). Plural suffixes attract the stress (his example xumba / xumbá 'nose', sg./pl.). No rule for where the stress falls within the word is given; Hetzron gives a position rule only for Xamir ('one of the last two syllables, conditioned by vowel quality'), not for Kemant.
new_statements.exceptions: Some words lose their stress in context; plural suffixes are stressed (stress moves onto the suffix).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('all words have stress in isolation'); loss of stress 'in context' points to phrase-level deaccenting. Data are H.-J. Sasse's unpublished field notes on Kemant proper (private communication to Hetzron), not Hetzron's own fieldwork.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog qima1242 bundles Kemant proper (Kärkär/Chilga, the variety in Appleyard 1975, Zelealem 2003 and Sasse's data used by Hetzron 1976), the Qwara dialect (Reinisch 1885, from Ethiopic-script Bible translations) and the Falasha/Kayla dialect (Halévy 1873). Hetzron's stress remark concerns Kemant proper (Sasse's notes). PHOIBLE's inventory 1161 attached to qima1242 is Hetzron 1969 on Southern Agaw = Awngi (awng1244), a misattribution, so its tone marks say nothing about Kemant.

new_statements.quote: A more promising area is Agaw. However, here, too, there are problems; only two Agaw languages (Awngi and Bilin) appear to have a tonal accent system comparable with LEC, whilst the other languages that have been studied in recent years (Kemant and Khamtanga) may have moved, or be moving towards a predictable, syllable-counting stress-based system, perhaps under the influence of Ethiopian Semitic.

However, here, too, there are problems; only two Agaw languages (Awngi and Bilin) appear to have a tonal accent system comparable with LEC, whilst the other languages that have been studied in recent years (Kemant and Khamtanga) may have moved, or be moving towards a predictable, syllable-counting stress-based system, perhaps under the influence of Ethiopian Semitic.' word for word ( line 549-555 has scanned noise 'Keinant', 'Khanitanga'; the page scan is clean). a full-text search for stres…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with Hetzron 1976 ('Kemant has only stress'; all words stressed in isolation) and adds the characterization 'predictable, syllable-counting stress-based system'; like Hetzron it gives no position, so the catalog's empty rule stays empty. Appleyard is the Kemant fieldworker (Kärkär dialect, 1973-4).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kemant (with Xamtanga) is said, with hedging ('may have moved, or be moving'), to have or be developing a predictable, syllable-counting stress system rather than the tonal accent of Awngi and Bilin; the position of the stress is not stated anywhere in the paper. The rest of the paper is about tonal accent in Somali, Afar, Oromo, Beja, Bilin and Awngi; Kemant appears otherwise only for case marking (p. 12), the jussive (p. 29) and in the bibliography (p. 30).
new_statements.exceptions: None; the whole statement is hedged ('may have moved, or be moving towards'), and attributed possibly to Ethiopian Semitic influence.
new_statements.identity_note: Appleyard's Kemant data come from his 1973-4 fieldwork on the Kärkär dialect (Appleyard 1975 is in the paper's bibliography); Hetzron's Kemant data are from H.-J. Sasse's unpublished notes. Halévy 1873 describes the Falasha/Kayla dialects of Dembea and Kwara, which he treats as the same speech as that of the Qemmantes (p. 156); it is not a description of Kemant proper.

readall_conflicts: No disagreement among the sources that could be opened. Hetzron 1976 (already in the catalog) says Kemant has stress, not tone, that all words carry stress in isolation but some lose it in context (possibly a trace of an older tonal system) and that plural suffixes are stressed; Appleyard 1991 says Kemant and Xamtanga 'may have moved, or be moving towards a predictable, syllable-counting stress-based system', which is consistent with Hetzron's older-tone hypothesis and adds 'predictable, syllable-counting'. Neither gives the position of the stress. Halévy 1873 is silent; Conti Rossini 1912 could not be opened.
